title: Buying a Premium Home in Bengaluru: A Practical Guide
seoTitle: Buying a Premium Home in Bengaluru: A Practical Guide
metaDescription: A calm, step-by-step guide to buying a premium home in Bengaluru: defining needs, shortlisting zones, evaluating projects and checking documents.
excerpt: From defining what premium means to you, to shortlisting, due diligence and financing, a measured approach to buying a home in Bengaluru.
bodyHtml:
Buying a premium home is rarely a single decision. It is a sequence of smaller ones: where to live, what kind of home suits the next decade of your life, which developer to trust, how to structure the finances, and when to commit. In a city as large and varied as Bengaluru, each of those choices has more than one reasonable answer. This guide sets out a practical order of operations so that the process feels considered rather than rushed.

Start with how you want to live, not with what is on the market

The word premium is used loosely in property marketing. Before looking at listings, it helps to decide what it means for you. For some households it is a larger floor plate and generous ceilings. For others it is the quality of common spaces, the density of the development, the amount of green cover, or the simple reassurance of a well-run community. A short written list of priorities, ranked honestly, is one of the most useful tools you can bring to a site visit.

Consider the practical dimensions as well:

  • Household shape. How many bedrooms do you need now, and how might that change with children, parents or a home office?
  • Commute and routine. Where do the adults work, where do children study, and how often do you travel from the airport?
  • Time horizon. Is this a home for the next five years or the next twenty-five? The answer affects how much weight to put on future infrastructure versus present convenience.
  • Apartment or villament. Low-rise, duplex-style villaments offer a house-like feel with shared amenities; apartments in a tower often offer views, efficiency and a wider choice of configurations.

Understand Bengaluru's zones before you shortlist

Bengaluru does not have a single centre of gravity. Employment is spread across several corridors, and each part of the city has developed its own character. North Bengaluru has grown around the airport corridor and established residential pockets such as Hennur and Yelahanka. East Bengaluru is anchored by Whitefield and the technology parks around it, with newer growth extending towards Hoskote. South and south-east Bengaluru, which includes Sarjapur Road, HSR Layout, Hosa Road and Electronic City, combines mature neighbourhoods with large, planned residential developments.

Rather than asking which zone is best, ask which zone fits the routine you described in the first step. A home that saves an hour of daily travel often matters more to long-term satisfaction than a marginally larger plan in an inconvenient location. If two or three zones seem plausible, visit each at different times of day and on a weekday as well as a weekend.

Set a realistic budget, including the costs around the price

The headline price of a home is only one component of the total outlay. A complete budget should account for:

  • The base price of the unit, usually expressed per square foot on a defined area.
  • Statutory charges such as stamp duty and registration fees, which are set by the state and change from time to time.
  • Goods and services tax where applicable to under-construction property.
  • Charges for parking, club membership, utility connections and legal processing, as itemised in the developer's cost sheet.
  • Maintenance deposits or advance maintenance, and the recurring monthly maintenance thereafter.
  • Interiors, furnishing and any customisation you plan to do after handover.

Ask every developer you consider for a complete cost sheet rather than a per-square-foot figure. Comparing projects on an all-in basis is the only fair comparison. If you plan to take a home loan, a pre-approval from your lender early in the process will clarify your ceiling and shorten the time between shortlisting and booking.

Shortlist developers, then projects

In a premium purchase, the developer matters as much as the plan. A developer's completed projects are the best evidence of what you will actually receive. Where possible, visit one or two of their delivered communities, walk the common areas, and speak to residents about construction quality, handover experience and how the community is maintained a few years on. Look for consistency of design thinking across projects: a developer with a clear point of view tends to deliver it reliably.

Once you trust the developer, evaluate the specific project. Study the master plan for how towers or villaments are positioned, how much of the land is left open, how vehicles and pedestrians are separated, and how daylight and ventilation reach each home. Read the specification sheet closely. The quality of flooring, fittings, windows and electrical systems is where premium projects differ most from ordinary ones.

Do the paperwork before the emotion takes over

By the time you have found a home you like, it is tempting to book first and verify later. Resist that. The Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act requires most projects above a size threshold to be registered with the state authority before they are marketed, and the project's RERA registration number should be displayed on its marketing material and listed on the official Karnataka RERA portal. Check the portal for the registered plans, the promoter details and the declared completion timeline.

Beyond RERA, a lawyer experienced in Karnataka property transactions should review the title documents, the sanctioned building plan, the land conversion status where relevant, and the draft agreement for sale. The small cost of independent legal advice is a sensible part of a premium purchase.

Visit with intention

A site visit is more than a tour of the show apartment. Bring your priority list and a few specific questions. Walk the actual location of the unit you are considering, not just the model home. Note the orientation of the balcony, the view from the main bedroom, the distance to lifts and the position of service areas. If the project is under construction, ask to see the current stage of work and the sample flat specifications side by side. If you are considering a villament, pay attention to the private garden or terrace, the privacy between neighbouring units and the entry sequence from the street.

Negotiate the structure, not only the price

Premium developers are usually more flexible on structure than on headline price. Discuss the payment schedule, the treatment of parking and club charges, the inclusion of specific fittings, and the timeline for registration. Ask what happens if there is a delay in possession, and make sure the answer is written into the agreement. Clarity now prevents friction later.

Plan for the years after the keys

Finally, think about life in the community. Ask how the resident association is formed, when maintenance responsibility transfers from the developer, what the maintenance corpus covers, and how common facilities are staffed. The experience of living in a premium development is shaped as much by how it is run as by how it was designed.

If you would like to see how these principles translate into real neighbourhoods, explore the Assetz developments across Bengaluru or speak with an advisor who can walk you through the options at your own pace.

title: North vs East vs South Bengaluru: What Buyers Should Consider
seoTitle: North vs East vs South Bengaluru: A Buyer's Comparison
metaDescription: How North, East and South Bengaluru differ in character, connectivity and housing, and a framework for choosing the zone that suits how you live and work.
excerpt: Each of Bengaluru's major residential zones has its own rhythm. Here is how to weigh North, East and South against the way you actually live.
bodyHtml:
Ask three Bengaluru residents where to buy a home and you will often receive three confident, contradictory answers. That is not because any of them is wrong. The city has grown outward along several corridors at once, and each has developed its own mix of employment, infrastructure and residential character. This article describes North, East and South Bengaluru in general terms and offers a way of thinking about which one fits you.

A city with several centres

Bengaluru's older core, around MG Road, Indiranagar, Jayanagar and Malleswaram, remains desirable but offers limited opportunity for new, large-format developments. Most premium new housing is therefore found in the growth corridors that radiate from the centre. Three of these dominate the conversation among buyers: the northern corridor towards the airport, the eastern corridor around Whitefield, and the southern and south-eastern corridor along Sarjapur Road, HSR Layout, Hosa Road and Electronic City.

Each corridor has a different balance of maturity and momentum. Understanding that balance is more useful than any single ranking.

North Bengaluru: the airport corridor

North Bengaluru's identity is closely tied to Kempegowda International Airport and the infrastructure that has grown along the route to it. Neighbourhoods such as Hennur, Thanisandra, Yelahanka, Hebbal and Jakkur sit along or near this corridor. Hennur Main Road in particular has developed into a residential spine with schools, hospitals and retail accompanying the housing.

The character of the north tends to be lower in density than the east, with lakes and established tree cover giving several pockets a settled, green feel. Business parks in and around the corridor have brought employment closer to home for many residents, and the airport proximity suits households that travel frequently.

Buyers considering the north should look closely at:

  • How the specific site connects to the main arterial roads, since internal roads vary in width and condition.
  • The maturity of social infrastructure immediately around the project, which can differ markedly from one pocket to the next.
  • Planned public transport extensions, which should be verified against official sources rather than marketing claims.

East Bengaluru: Whitefield and beyond

East Bengaluru is the city's longest-established technology corridor. Whitefield, the International Tech Park and the surrounding business campuses have attracted employment for decades, and housing, schools, hospitals, hotels and retail have grown around them. The result is a zone that feels mature and self-contained, where many residents live, work and socialise within a relatively compact area.

That maturity also means that land within Whitefield itself is scarce, and newer large-format developments have moved outward towards Hoskote and the areas along the old Madras road. These newer locations offer more space and a quieter setting, with the trade-off that social infrastructure is still catching up in places.

Points to weigh in the east:

  • Whether your routine is contained within the corridor or requires regular travel across the city, since east-west journeys at peak hours demand patience.
  • The difference between living inside the established core and in an emerging pocket further out, in terms of both daily convenience and the feel of the neighbourhood.
  • The density and scale of the development, since the east has a mix of very large townships and smaller communities.

South and south-east Bengaluru: Sarjapur Road, HSR, Hosa Road and Electronic City

The south and south-east combine some of the city's most established residential neighbourhoods with its largest zone of planned new housing. HSR Layout and Koramangala are mature, walkable and well served by everything a household needs, while Sarjapur Road has developed into a long residential corridor with schools, hospitals and office campuses along its length. Hosa Road and the areas around Electronic City extend this pattern further south, where large technology campuses provide a stable employment base.

The appeal of this zone is breadth of choice. Buyers can find everything from compact apartments near HSR Layout to expansive villa and villament communities further along Sarjapur Road. The zone also benefits from being relatively well connected to both the eastern technology corridor and the city centre.

Considerations in the south and south-east:

  • Road capacity on the main corridors is under constant pressure, so the exact position of a project relative to junctions and alternative routes matters.
  • Lake rejuvenation and buffer-zone rules affect what can be built in certain pockets; a project's compliance with these should be verified.
  • The pace of change is high, which means both opportunity and construction activity in the surrounding area for some years.

A framework for choosing

Rather than asking which zone is best, map the following against each one:

1. The journeys you make most often

List the five journeys your household makes every week, such as to work, school, family and the airport. Estimate them honestly for each zone at the times you actually travel. The zone that minimises the sum of these journeys deserves the most weight.

2. The maturity you need today

Households with young children or elderly parents often need schools, clinics and daily retail within easy reach from day one. Others are comfortable waiting a few years for a neighbourhood to fill in. Be honest about which you are.

3. The kind of community you want

A compact, walkable neighbourhood and a spacious low-density community are both valid preferences, but they are rarely found in the same place. Decide which one matters more.

4. Your time horizon

The longer you plan to live in the home, the more weight you can give to a zone's direction of travel over its present state. If you expect to move within a few years, prioritise what exists now.

Visit before you decide

Zones are generalisations; sites are specific. Two projects a short distance apart can offer very different daily experiences. Visit any shortlisted location on a weekday morning, a weekday evening and a weekend, and walk the surroundings rather than only driving through. Pay attention to noise, light, the condition of approach roads and how the development sits within its neighbourhood.

Assetz has developments in North, East and South Bengaluru, which makes it straightforward to compare zones with a single advisor. Explore the portfolio or arrange a visit to the locations that match your shortlist.

title: How to Evaluate a Residential Project Before Booking
seoTitle: How to Evaluate a Residential Project Before Booking
metaDescription: A structured checklist for evaluating a residential project before booking: developer record, land approvals, master plan, specifications and terms.
excerpt: Booking a home is a commitment. This structured checklist helps you assess the developer, the land, the plan and the paperwork before you sign.
bodyHtml:
A booking is the point at which interest becomes commitment. Before it, you are free to walk away; after it, changing your mind has a cost in time, money and energy. The evaluation that precedes a booking is therefore the most valuable work in the entire purchase. This article sets out a structured way to do it, moving from the developer to the land, the plan, the home itself and finally the terms.

1. The developer

A project is a promise made by a developer. The most reliable way to judge the promise is to look at how previous promises were kept.

  • Delivered projects. Visit at least one completed development by the same developer. Walk the common areas, look at how the facade and landscaping have aged, and notice whether the amenities shown in the original brochure exist and are in use.
  • Resident experience. Speak to residents about handover, snagging and how responsive the developer was in the first year. Resident associations are usually candid.
  • Consistency. A developer with a clear design philosophy tends to apply it across projects. Look for that consistency rather than for a single standout.
  • Financial discipline. Under RERA, a significant share of money collected from buyers must be held in a separate account and used for that project's construction. Ask how the developer manages this and whether construction funding is in place.

2. The land and its approvals

Many of the problems that surface years after purchase originate in the land. The questions to ask are straightforward, even if the documents behind them are not.

  • Title. Does the developer own the land, or hold it under a joint development agreement with the owner? Either is common; what matters is that the chain of ownership is clear and documented.
  • Land use. Has agricultural land been converted for residential use where required, and is the land within the zone permitted for this kind of development under the applicable master plan?
  • Sanctioned plan. Has the building plan been sanctioned by the relevant planning authority, and does the project being marketed match the plan that was sanctioned?
  • Environmental and other clearances. Larger projects require environmental clearance, and projects near lakes, nalas or other sensitive features must respect buffer zones. Ask which clearances apply and whether they have been obtained.
  • RERA registration. Confirm the project's registration on the official Karnataka RERA portal and compare the registered details, including the promoter, the number of units and the declared completion date, with what you have been told.

Have a lawyer with Karnataka experience review these documents. A developer confident in its paperwork will make them available without hesitation.

3. The master plan

The master plan is the single most informative drawing in any project. It shows how the land has been used and, by implication, what the developer values.

  • Open space. How much of the site is left unbuilt, and is that open space usable, landscaped and reachable from most homes, or fragmented into leftover strips?
  • Density. How many homes share the site, the lifts, the clubhouse and the parking? Lower density generally means a calmer community but a higher share of maintenance per home.
  • Orientation. How are the blocks positioned relative to the sun and prevailing breeze? Good orientation reduces heat gain and the need for artificial cooling.
  • Movement. Are vehicles kept to the perimeter or basements so that the heart of the development is for people? How far is the walk from the main gate to the furthest home?
  • Services. Where are the sewage treatment plant, generators, transformer yard and waste collection points? These are necessary, but you should know which homes are nearest to them.

4. The home itself

Having understood the context, turn to the specific unit.

Plan and proportion

Study the floor plan with a scale rule, not just by impression. Check the usable dimensions of each room, the size and position of windows, the depth of balconies, and whether the layout creates wasted corridor space. Ask for the carpet area as defined under RERA, which is the area you will actually live in, and compare it with the super built-up area on which the price is quoted.

Light, air and privacy

Trace which rooms face which direction and what each window looks onto. Cross-ventilation, a kitchen that can be vented, and bedrooms that do not face directly into a neighbour's are details that matter every day.

Specifications

The specification sheet lists the materials and brands used for flooring, doors, windows, kitchen counters, sanitary ware, electrical fittings and security systems. Compare it line by line with the show apartment and ask which items are indicative and which are committed. Premium projects distinguish themselves most clearly here.

Structure and services

Ask about the structural system, the quality of waterproofing, the provision for water supply and storage, rainwater harvesting, power backup and fibre connectivity. These are not glamorous, but they determine how the home performs over decades.

5. The terms

Finally, read the documents that govern the relationship between you and the developer.

  • Cost sheet. Confirm that every charge is itemised and that there are no open-ended items. Understand what is included in the base price and what is additional.
  • Payment schedule. In a construction-linked plan, payments should be tied to clearly defined construction milestones. Check that the milestones are objective and verifiable.
  • Agreement for sale. Read the draft agreement in full, including the clauses on possession date, delay compensation, the process for changes in specification, the formation of the owners' association and the handling of defects after handover. Under RERA, the developer is responsible for structural and workmanship defects for a defined period after possession.
  • Exit terms. Understand what happens if you need to cancel after booking and before registration, and what deductions apply.

Bringing it together

No project will score perfectly on every point, and that is not the goal. The goal is to know where the compromises are before you book, so that you choose them rather than discover them. Organise your findings under the five headings above, note the questions that remain unanswered, and put those questions to the developer in writing. The quality of the answers is itself a useful signal.

Assetz advisors are happy to walk through each of these points for any development in the portfolio. Explore the projects or request a conversation to begin your own evaluation.

title: Understanding Carpet Area, Built-Up Area and Super Built-Up Area
seoTitle: Carpet Area vs Built-Up vs Super Built-Up Area Explained
metaDescription: What carpet area, built-up area and super built-up area mean, how RERA defines carpet area, and how to compare homes and prices on a like-for-like basis.
excerpt: Three area terms appear on every brochure and cost sheet. Knowing exactly what each one measures is the key to comparing homes fairly.
bodyHtml:
Few things cause more confusion in an Indian home purchase than the word area. A brochure may quote one number, the cost sheet another, and the agreement a third, each describing the same home. The three terms behind these numbers, carpet area, built-up area and super built-up area, are not interchangeable, and the differences between them can be substantial. Understanding them allows you to compare homes and prices on a genuinely like-for-like basis.

Carpet area: the space you live in

Carpet area is, in everyday terms, the floor area inside the walls of your home. It is the space on which a carpet could in principle be laid: bedrooms, living and dining areas, kitchen, bathrooms, passages and store rooms.

The Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act gives carpet area a formal definition. Under the Act, carpet area is the net usable floor area of an apartment, excluding the area covered by external walls, areas under service shafts, exclusive balcony or verandah areas and exclusive open terrace areas, but including the area covered by the internal partition walls of the apartment. The Act requires developers to disclose carpet area and to sell on that basis, which has made it the most consistent and comparable measure available to buyers.

Two practical points follow from the definition:

  • Balconies and terraces are stated separately from carpet area. A home with generous balconies will have a carpet area that understates the total space you can use, so ask for both figures.
  • Because internal partition walls are included, two homes with identical carpet area can have slightly different usable room sizes depending on how many internal walls they have.

Built-up area: the home including its walls

Built-up area is the carpet area plus the thickness of the walls that enclose the home and, in most usage, the area of balconies and other exclusive spaces attached to it. It represents the footprint of the apartment as a physical object rather than the space inside it.

Built-up area is not defined in RERA and is used less often in formal documents than it once was, but it still appears on some cost sheets and in some lenders' valuations. When you see it, ask precisely what has been included, since practices vary from one developer to another.

Super built-up area: the home plus its share of common spaces

Super built-up area adds to the built-up area a proportionate share of the common areas of the building or development. Depending on the project, this can include lobbies, corridors, staircases, lift shafts and lift lobbies, the clubhouse, and sometimes other shared facilities. Each apartment is allocated a share of these spaces, usually in proportion to its size, and the result is added to its built-up area.

The difference between carpet area and super built-up area is often described as the loading factor. It is a matter of design and of convention rather than regulation, and it can differ noticeably between projects. A development with wide corridors, grand lobbies and a large clubhouse will typically carry a higher loading than a simpler one. Neither is inherently better; the point is that you should know what you are paying for.

Why the distinction matters when comparing prices

Price per square foot is the standard shorthand for comparing homes, but it is only meaningful if the square feet being compared are measured the same way. Consider two homes quoted at similar prices per square foot on super built-up area. If one carries a noticeably higher loading than the other, its price per square foot of carpet area, the space you will actually occupy, is correspondingly higher. The brochure comparison would have suggested parity; the carpet-area comparison reveals the difference.

To compare fairly:

  • Ask every developer for the RERA carpet area, the exclusive balcony area and the super built-up area of each unit you are considering.
  • Divide the total price, including all charges on the cost sheet, by the carpet area to arrive at an all-in price per square foot of usable space.
  • Note the loading factor as a separate piece of information. A higher loading may reflect generous common areas that you will value, or simply a wider corridor; the master plan and a site visit will tell you which.

What RERA changed

Before RERA, homes were commonly marketed and sold on super built-up area, with the method of calculating common-area shares left to the developer. Buyers had no consistent way to know how much of the quoted area was inside their front door. RERA's requirement to disclose carpet area, and its precise definition of the term, shifted the basis of comparison to a measure buyers can verify.

In practice, many developers continue to quote prices on super built-up area while disclosing carpet area alongside it, which the law permits as long as the carpet area is clearly stated. The habit worth forming as a buyer is to translate every quote into carpet-area terms before comparing.

Reading a floor plan with these terms in mind

A floor plan drawn to scale will show dimensions of each room. Multiplying length by width for every room and passage and adding the results gives you an approximation of carpet area, usually slightly lower than the official figure because the official figure includes internal walls. Doing this exercise once is a useful check on the numbers you have been given and a good way to develop a feel for how a quoted area translates into rooms you can picture.

While you are at it, check:

  • Whether the plan shows wall thicknesses, which helps distinguish carpet from built-up area.
  • Whether balcony and utility areas are marked and dimensioned separately.
  • Whether any area labelled as a terrace or garden is exclusive to the unit or shared.

Questions to put to a developer

  • What is the RERA carpet area of this unit, and what is the exclusive balcony area?
  • On which area is the quoted price per square foot based?
  • What common areas are included in the super built-up area, and how is each unit's share calculated?
  • Will the carpet area be stated in the agreement for sale, and what happens if the final measured area differs from the agreed figure?

The last question is important. RERA contemplates adjustment of the price if the carpet area at handover differs from what was agreed, and the agreement should set out how any such variation will be handled.

In summary

Carpet area is the space inside your home and the measure RERA requires developers to disclose. Built-up area adds the walls and exclusive attached spaces. Super built-up area adds a share of the common areas. Prices are often quoted on the last of these, but the fairest comparison between homes is made on the first. Once you are fluent in the three terms, cost sheets and brochures become far easier to read.

title: The Role of Green Spaces in Contemporary Residential Design
seoTitle: Green Spaces in Contemporary Residential Design
metaDescription: Why green space has moved from the margins of residential design to its centre, and what buyers should look for in the landscape of a new development.
excerpt: Landscape is no longer an afterthought in good residential design. Here is what thoughtful green space does for a community, and how to recognise it.
bodyHtml:
For much of the past few decades, the landscape in a residential development was whatever remained after the buildings, roads and parking had been placed. A lawn here, a row of palms there, a children's play area tucked beside the generator room. Contemporary residential design has reversed that order of priorities. In the best new communities, the open space is planned first and the buildings are arranged to serve it.

Why green space has moved to the centre

Several things have converged. Residents in dense cities have become more conscious of the effect of their surroundings on wellbeing, and the evidence that regular contact with greenery supports mental and physical health has become difficult to ignore. Climate concerns have made the practical functions of landscape, such as shade, cooling, stormwater absorption and biodiversity, matter in a way they did not before. And buyers have begun to compare projects on the quality of their shared outdoor spaces, not only on the finishes inside the home.

In Bengaluru specifically, the city's identity as a garden city and the memory of its tree-lined streets give green space a cultural resonance. Developments that work with the existing terrain, retain mature trees and plant with native species feel like a continuation of the city rather than an interruption of it.

What good green space does

  • It cools. Tree canopy and planted ground absorb less heat than paved surfaces and release moisture, lowering ambient temperatures around homes and reducing reliance on air conditioning.
  • It manages water. Permeable landscapes and planted swales slow rainfall, allow it to recharge the ground and reduce the load on drains, which matters in a city with intense monsoon showers.
  • It structures movement. A central green with paths through it encourages walking between homes and amenities and gives children a safe place to play within sight of adults.
  • It creates community. Shared gardens, shaded seating and open lawns are where neighbours meet without having to arrange it.
  • It supports life beyond people. Native planting, water bodies and undisturbed corners bring birds, butterflies and pollinators into the development.

How to recognise thoughtful landscape design

When you study a master plan or walk a site, a few indicators separate genuine landscape thinking from decoration.

Continuity. Is the open space a connected whole that you can walk through, or a set of disconnected fragments between towers? Continuous green is usable; fragmented green is mostly visual.

Ground-level priority. Are vehicles kept to the perimeter or in basements so that the ground plane belongs to people and planting? Developments that achieve this feel markedly calmer.

Mature and native planting. Has the plan retained existing trees where possible, and does the planting palette favour species suited to Bengaluru's climate that will thrive without excessive water?

Variety of experience. A good landscape offers different kinds of outdoor space: a quiet garden, an active lawn, a shaded walk, a water feature, a place to sit alone and a place to gather.

Private green for each home. In villaments and low-rise formats, the quality of the private garden or terrace, and the planting that screens it from neighbours, is as important as the shared landscape.

Questions to ask

  • What proportion of the site is open and landscaped, and how much of that is usable rather than ornamental?
  • How is the landscape irrigated, and is treated water reused for the purpose?
  • Who maintains the landscape after handover, and is a long-term maintenance plan in place?
  • How were existing trees and natural features treated in the plan?

Landscape is central to how Assetz plans its communities. Explore the developments to see how green space shapes each one, or speak with an advisor about the approach taken at a particular location.

title: Essential Documents to Review Before Purchasing a Home
seoTitle: Essential Documents to Review Before Buying a Home
metaDescription: The key documents to review before buying a home in Karnataka: title, sanctioned plans, RERA registration, the cost sheet and the agreement for sale.
excerpt: A concise guide to the documents that underpin a safe home purchase, and what to look for in each.
bodyHtml:
The documents behind a home purchase are less interesting than the home, but they are what you are actually buying. A well-designed apartment on land with an unclear title is a problem, not an asset. This guide lists the documents that a buyer, with the help of a qualified lawyer, should review before committing. It is general in nature and does not replace professional advice for a specific transaction.

Documents relating to the land

  • Title documents. The chain of ownership showing how the current owner or developer came to hold the land, usually traced back over several decades through sale deeds, gift deeds, partition deeds or inheritance records.
  • Encumbrance certificate. A record from the sub-registrar's office listing registered transactions affecting the property over a given period, used to check for mortgages or other claims.
  • Khata and tax records. Municipal records establishing that the property is recognised by the local authority and that property tax has been paid.
  • Land conversion order. Where the land was previously agricultural, the order permitting its use for residential purposes.
  • Joint development agreement. If the developer is building on land owned by someone else, the agreement between them, along with the registered power of attorney, should be reviewed to confirm the developer's right to sell.

Documents relating to the project

  • Sanctioned building plan. The plan approved by the relevant planning authority. The project being marketed should match it in height, number of units and layout.
  • Commencement certificate. Permission from the authority to begin construction.
  • RERA registration certificate. Projects above the statutory size threshold must be registered with the Karnataka Real Estate Regulatory Authority. The registration number should appear on all marketing, and the registration details, including the promoter, approved plans and declared completion date, can be checked on the official Karnataka RERA portal.
  • Environmental and other clearances. Depending on the project's scale and location, clearances from environmental, fire, airport, pollution control or other authorities may be required.
  • No-objection certificates. From utility providers and other bodies as applicable.

Documents relating to your purchase

  • Cost sheet. An itemised statement of the total price, including base price, charges for parking, clubhouse, utilities and legal processing, statutory taxes and duties, and any deposits.
  • Payment schedule. The timing of each payment, linked in a construction-linked plan to specific stages of work.
  • Booking or allotment letter. Issued on booking, confirming the unit, the price and the key terms.
  • Agreement for sale. The principal contract between you and the developer. Under RERA it must follow a prescribed form and should set out the carpet area, the possession date, delay compensation, the specifications, the defect liability period and the terms for the owners' association.
  • Sale deed. The document registered at the sub-registrar's office that transfers ownership to you. Stamp duty and registration fees are payable at this stage at rates set by the state.

Documents at handover

  • Occupancy certificate. Issued by the authority once the building is complete and found to comply with the sanctioned plan and applicable rules. Possession should ordinarily follow this certificate.
  • Completion certificate. Confirming that construction has been completed in accordance with the approved plan.
  • Possession letter and handover documents. Including keys, warranties for fittings and equipment, and the snag list process.

A note on process

Ask the developer for the full set of documents before booking, not after. Have them reviewed by a lawyer with experience in Karnataka property law, and if you are taking a home loan, remember that the lender's legal team will review them as well, which provides a second check. Keep copies of everything, including correspondence, in a single organised file.

Assetz makes project documentation available to prospective buyers on request. Explore the developments or speak with an advisor to begin your review.
